hints: Look closely at the ring structure, especially the OH groups on carbon 1 (right side) and carbon 2 (bottom right). Which hexose has this exact arrangement?
Remember what amylopectin, glycogen and sucrose are each made from. Which single monomer is found in both alpha-glucose polysaccharides and in this common disaccharide?
walkthrough:
**Identify the monomer**

First, recognise this as a hexose sugar in its ring form. The positions of the OH groups, with the OH on carbon 1 pointing down and the OH on carbon 2 pointing down, match alpha-glucose.

This is the key building block to look for, not beta-glucose which is used to make cellulose.

**Recall what each molecule contains**

Amylopectin is a branched polysaccharide made only of alpha-glucose joined by 1,4 and 1,6 glycosidic bonds. Glycogen is the animal storage polysaccharide, also made only of alpha-glucose with the same bond types but more branching.

Sucrose is a disaccharide made of alpha-glucose joined to fructose.

**Use the Venn diagram**

Since alpha-glucose is present in amylopectin AND in glycogen AND in sucrose, it must sit in the centre where all three circles overlap. That central region is labelled B.

options.A: Region A is only amylopectin and glycogen. This misses sucrose, which also contains alpha-glucose, so it is incomplete.
options.B: Region B is the overlap of all three circles. Amylopectin, glycogen and sucrose all contain alpha-glucose, so this is correct.
options.C: Region C is only amylopectin and sucrose. This wrongly leaves out glycogen, which is also a polymer of alpha-glucose.
options.D: Region D is sucrose only. This is wrong because alpha-glucose is also the monomer for both amylopectin and glycogen.
